claim: ZNRF2 interacts with mTOR on membranes
source: In this study, we show that ZNRF2 interacts with mTOR on membranes, promoting the amino acid-stimulated translocation of mTORC1 to lysosomes and its activation in human cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments showing co-purification of mTOR with ZNRF2-GFP (Figure 1a,b) and mass spectrometry identification of mTOR in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates.

claim: ZNRF2 promotes amino acid-stimulated translocation of mTORC1 to lysosomes
source: In this study, we show that ZNRF2 interacts with mTOR on membranes, promoting the amino acid-stimulated translocation of mTORC1 to lysosomes and its activation in human cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing decreased mTOR-LAMP2 colocalization upon ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 3b,c).

claim: ZNRF2 interacts with the V-ATPase
source: ZNRF2 also interacts with the V-ATPase and preserves lysosomal acidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry identification of V-ATPase components in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates (Figure 4a) and Western blot confirmation (Figure 4b).

claim: ZNRF2 preserves lysosomal acidity
source: ZNRF2 also interacts with the V-ATPase and preserves lysosomal acidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements showing increased lysosomal pH from 4.3 to 5.5 upon ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 5f).

claim: Knockdown of ZNRF2 decreases cell size
source: Moreover, knockdown of ZNRF2 decreases cell size and cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry measurements of cell size (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).

claim: Knockdown of ZNRF2 decreases cell proliferation
source: Moreover, knockdown of ZNRF2 decreases cell size and cell proliferation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assays showing decreased proliferation in ZNRF2 knockdown cells (Figure 3d).

claim: mTORC1 phosphorylates ZNRF2 on Ser145 upon growth factor and amino acid stimulation
source: Upon growth factor and amino acid stimulation, mTORC1 phosphorylates ZNRF2 on Ser145, and this phosphosite is dephosphorylated by protein phosphatase 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assays (Figure 1d,e), mass spectrometry identification of phospho-Ser145, and Western blotting with phospho-specific antibodies showing rapamycin-sensitive phosphorylation (Figure 1g,h).

claim: Protein phosphatase 6 dephosphorylates ZNRF2 at Ser145
source: Upon growth factor and amino acid stimulation, mTORC1 phosphorylates ZNRF2 on Ser145, and this phosphosite is dephosphorylated by protein phosphatase 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphatase assays showing PP6 dephosphorylates phospho-Ser145 (Figure 2d) and cellular experiments showing rapamycin-induced dephosphorylation is rescued by PPP6C knockdown (Figure 2e,f).

claim: Ser145 phosphorylation stimulates vesicle-to-cytosol translocation of ZNRF2
source: Ser145 phosphorylation stimulates vesicle-to-cytosol translocation of ZNRF2 and forms a novel negative feedback on mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by previous work (Hoxhaj et al., 2012) showing Ser145Ala mutation hampers IGF1-stimulated cytosolic translocation, and by imaging data showing rapamycin increases membranal localization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).

claim: Ser145 phosphorylation forms a novel negative feedback on mTORC1
source: Ser145 phosphorylation stimulates vesicle-to-cytosol translocation of ZNRF2 and forms a novel negative feedback on mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing overexpression of ZNRF2-Ser145Ala enhances mTORC1 activation by amino acids more than wild-type ZNRF2 (Figure 2g).

claim: ZNRF2 acts upstream of Rag-GTPases and the V-ATPase to activate mTORC1
source: Our findings uncover ZNRF2 as a component of the amino acid sensing machinery that acts upstream of Rag-GTPases and the V-ATPase to activate mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing constitutively active Rag mutants rescue mTORC1 activity in ZNRF2 knockdown cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c) and by ZNRF2's effects on V-ATPase function and localization.

claim: mTOR binds to ZNRF2-GFP but not to GFP-only control
source: The interactions of mTOR with ZNRF2 was confirmed by Western blotting, which showed that endogenous mTOR bind to ZNRF2-GFP, but not to the GFP-only control nor to an N-myristoylation-defective mutant (G2A) of ZNRF2 (Hoxhaj et al., 2012), indicating that N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is important for this interaction (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is directly supported by Western blot data in Figure 1a showing mTOR co-immunoprecipitates with ZNRF2-GFP but not GFP control.

claim: N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is important for mTOR interaction
source: The interactions of mTOR with ZNRF2 was confirmed by Western blotting, which showed that endogenous mTOR bind to ZNRF2-GFP, but not to the GFP-only control nor to an N-myristoylation-defective mutant (G2A) of ZNRF2 (Hoxhaj et al., 2012), indicating that N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is important for this interaction (Figure 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing mTOR does not bind to G2A-ZNRF2 mutant (Figure 1a).

claim: ZNRF2 interacts with raptor and mLST8
source: ZNRF2 also interacted with other components of the mTORC1 complex, namely raptor and mLST8 (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing co-purification of raptor and mLST8 with ZNRF2-GFP (Figure 1b).

claim: ZNRF2 shows co-localization with mTOR in HEK293 cells
source: ZNRF2 also interacted with other components of the mTORC1 complex, namely raptor and mLST8 (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and showed co-localization with mTOR in HEK293 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).

claim: Raptor, rictor, Sin1 and mLST8 do not mediate the binding of ZNRF2 to mTOR
source: ZNRF2 interacted with mTOR under all these conditions, indicating that raptor, rictor, Sin1 and mLST8 do not mediate the binding of ZNRF2 to mTOR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation experiments in cells depleted of Raptor or lacking rictor, Sin1, and mLST8 showing maintained ZNRF2-mTOR interaction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e,f).

claim: mTOR binds to both the N-terminal (1 to 156) region of ZNRF2 and C-terminal RING domain-containing region of ZNRF2, provided these fragments carry an N-terminal myristoyl group
source: mTOR bound to both the N-terminal (1 to 156) region of ZNRF2 and C-terminal RING (catalytic) domain-containing region of ZNRF2, provided these fragments also carried an N-terminal myristoyl group (Figure 1c)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with ZNRF2 fragments (Figure 1c).

claim: mTOR cannot interact with ZNRF2 with a defective UBZ domain (Cys160Ala/Cys163Ala mutations)
source: but was not able to interact to ZNRF2 with a defective UBZ domain (Cys160Ala/Cys163Ala mutations) or to the RING domain alone (residues 156-end).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing loss of mTOR binding to UBZ mutant (Figure 1c).

claim: Membranal localization is required for the mTOR-ZNRF2 interaction
source: These data indicate that membranal localization is required for the mTOR-ZNRF2 interaction, consistent with lack of mTOR binding to non-N- myristoylated ZNRF2 (Figure 1a)
evidence: The claim is inferred from data showing N-myristoylation is required for mTOR binding and that multiple domains contribute to the interaction.

claim: mTOR can phosphorylate ZNRF2-GST in vitro
source: mTOR could phosphorylate ZNRF2-GST in vitro, and this was prevented by the mTOR-specific inhibitor Ku-0063794 (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing radioactive phosphate incorporation into ZNRF2-GST (Figure 1d).

claim: Ku-0063794 prevents mTOR phosphorylation of ZNRF2-GST in vitro
source: mTOR could phosphorylate ZNRF2-GST in vitro, and this was prevented by the mTOR-specific inhibitor Ku-0063794 (Figure 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data showing loss of phosphorylation in the presence of Ku-0063794 (Figure 1d).

claim: Mass spectrometric analysis revealed Ser145 as a single phosphorylated residue in ZNRF2 phosphorylated by mTOR in vitro
source: Mass spectrometric analysis revealed a single phosphorylated residue, namely Ser145 (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data showing phospho-Ser145 peptide (Figure 1e).

claim: Ser145 is conserved only in vertebrate ZNRF2 proteins
source: Though ZNRF2 is conserved across eukaryotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a–c), Ser145 is conserved only in the vertebrate proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).

claim: The mTOR catalytic inhibitor Ku-0063794 decreases Ser145 phosphorylation in response to IGF1
source: In cells, the mTOR catalytic inhibitor, Ku-0063794, decreased Ser145 phosphorylation in response to IGF1 (Figure 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing dose-dependent decrease in phospho-Ser145 with Ku-0063794 treatment (Figure 1f).

claim: mTORC1 is solely responsible for amino acid-stimulated phosphorylation of Ser145
source: However, while mTORC1 is solely responsible for amino acid-stimulated phosphorylation of Ser145, rapamycin decreased, but did not abolish Ser145 phosphorylation in response to IGF1 (Figures 1g)
evidence: The claim is supported by complete rapamycin sensitivity of amino acid-induced Ser145 phosphorylation (Figure 1g,h).

claim: Another IGF1-activated kinase can also phosphorylate Ser145
source: However, while mTORC1 is solely responsible for amino acid-stimulated phosphorylation of Ser145, rapamycin decreased, but did not abolish Ser145 phosphorylation in response to IGF1 (Figures 1g), which suggests that another IGF1-activated kinase can also phosphorylate this site.
evidence: The claim is inferred from partial rapamycin sensitivity of IGF1-induced Ser145 phosphorylation (Figure 1g).

claim: ZNRF2 is directly phosphorylated by mTORC1 rather than via S6K
source: The phosphorylation of Ser145 was not affected by the p70 S6 kinase 1 (S6K1)-specific inhibitor PF-4708671 (Pearce et al., 2010), indicating that ZNRF2 is directly phosphorylated by mTORC1 rather than via S6K (Figure 1j).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing no effect of S6K1 inhibitor on Ser145 phosphorylation (Figure 1j).

claim: mTORC2 does not phosphorylate Ser145
source: Moreover, phosphorylation of Ser145 was not decreased in rictor or mLST8 knock-out MEFs, ruling out the possibility that mTORC2 phosphorylates this site (Figures 1k and 1l, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing maintained Ser145 phosphorylation in rictor and mLST8 knockout cells (Figure 1k,l).

claim: Ser145 of ZNRF2 is phosphorylated by mTORC1 in response to growth factors and amino acids
source: Together, these data are consistent with Ser145 of ZNRF2 being phosphorylated by mTORC1 in response to growth factors and amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple lines of evidence including in vitro kinase assays, rapamycin sensitivity, and lack of effect in mTORC2-deficient cells.

claim: Ser145Ala mutation hampered the IGF1-stimulated dissociation of ZNRF2 into the cytoplasm
source: Previously, we reported that ZNRF2 is translocated from intracellular membranes to the cytosol upon IGF1 stimulation and that Ser145Ala mutation hampered the IGF1-stimulated dissociation of ZNRF2 into the cytoplasm (Hoxhaj et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by previous published work (Hoxhaj et al., 2012).

claim: Rapamycin increased the membranal localization of ZNRF2-GFP
source: Consistent with mTORC1 being a Ser145 kinase, rapamycin increased the membranal localization of ZNRF2-GFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a; Hoxhaj et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing increased Golgi colocalization with rapamycin treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a).

claim: Ser145Ala mutation of ZNRF2 resulted in a more distinct membranal localization compared to wild-type protein
source: In addition, Ser145Ala mutation of ZNRF2 resulted in a more distinct membranal localization in comparison to the wild-type protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b).

claim: ZNRF2-GFP co-localized predominantly with Golgi and to a lesser extent with lysosomes
source: The expressed ZNRF2-GFP and Ser145Ala-ZNRF2-GFP co-localized predominantly with Golgi and to a lesser extent with the lysosomes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing colocalization with Golgi-RFP and Lysotracker (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a,b).

claim: Components of the protein serine/threonine phosphatase PP6 complex were identified as high-score hits in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates
source: In addition to mTOR, several components of the protein serine/threonine phosphatase PP6 complex were identified as high-score hits in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates analyzed by mass spectrometry (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).

claim: The PP6 holoenzyme comprises the catalytic subunit PPP6C, three regulatory subunits PP6R1/2/3, and three ankyrin repeat-domain containing regulatory subunits ANKRD28/44/52
source: The PP6 holoenzyme is a heteromeric complex, comprising the catalytic (PPP6C), three regulatory subunits PP6R1/2/3 (also called SIT4 phosphatase–associated protein (SAPS1/2/3) and three ankyrin repeat-domain containing regulatory subunits (ANKRD28/44/52) (Stefansson and Brautigan, 2006; Stefansson et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Stefansson and Brautigan, 2006; Stefansson et al., 2008).

claim: Binding of PP6 complex to ZNRF2 was unaffected by the position of the GFP tag
source: The binding of PP6 complex components to ZNRF2-GFP was unaffected by the position of the GFP tag (N- or C-terminus) suggesting that the N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is not required for the interaction of PP6 to ZNRF2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing PP6 binding to both N- and C-terminally tagged ZNRF2 (Figure 2a).

claim: N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is not required for the interaction of PP6 to ZNRF2
source: The binding of PP6 complex components to ZNRF2-GFP was unaffected by the position of the GFP tag (N- or C-terminus) suggesting that the N-myristoylation of ZNRF2 is not required for the interaction of PP6 to ZNRF2 (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that both N- and C-terminally tagged ZNRF2 bind PP6, where N-terminal tagging prevents myristoylation.

claim: Binding of the PP6 complex to ZNRF2 was compromised by the E3 ligase-dead (Cys199Ala) mutation
source: Interestingly, binding of the PP6 complex to ZNRF2 was compromised by the E3 ligase-dead (Cys199Ala) mutation (Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing reduced PP6 binding to C199A-ZNRF2 (Figure 2a).

claim: ZNRF2 lacking the catalytic RING domain (fragments 1–180 and 1–156) did not bind to PP6
source: Consistent with this, ZNRF2 lacking the catalytic RING domain (fragments 1–180 and 1–156) did not bind to PP6 (Figure 2b and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with ZNRF2 fragments (Figure 2b).

claim: Knockdown of PPP6C resulted in a decrease in the levels of other PP6 subunits in cell lysates
source: Only knockdown of PPP6C resulted in a decrease in the levels of other subunits in cell lysates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing decreased PP6 subunit levels upon PPP6C knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).

claim: Depletion of PPP6C, PP6R1 (SAPS1) and PP6R3 (SAPS3) did not affect the ability of other PP6 holoenzyme components to interact with ZNRF2
source: Depletion of PPP6C, PP6R1 (SAPS1) and PP6R3 (SAPS3) did not affect the ability of other PP6 holoenzyme components to interact with ZNRF2.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing maintained PP6 component binding to ZNRF2 upon knockdown of these subunits (Figure 2c).

claim: Knockdown of PP6R2 (SAPS2) and ANKRD28 decreased the amounts of PPP6C, SAPS1 and SAPS3 that co-immunoprecipitated with ZNRF2-GFP
source: In contrast, knockdown of PP6R2 (SAPS2) and ANKRD28 decreased the amounts of PPP6C, SAPS1 and SAPS3 that co-immunoprecipitated with ZNRF2-GFP.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing reduced PP6 component binding upon SAPS2 and ANKRD28 knockdown (Figure 2c).

claim: SAPS2 and ANKRD28 mediate the interaction of the PP6 complex with ZNRF2
source: These data suggest that SAPS2 and ANKRD28 mediate the interaction of the PP6 complex with ZNRF2 (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is inferred from knockdown experiments showing these subunits are required for PP6 complex binding to ZNRF2 (Figure 2c).

claim: The yeast orthologue of PP6 (Sit4) functions downstream of the rapamycin-sensitive TOR complex 1
source: The yeast orthologue of PP6 (Sit4), functions downstream of the rapamycin-sensitive TOR complex 1 to regulate G1 to S phase cell cycle progression, Gcn2-regulated translation and expression of certain nitrogen catabolite-repressed genes (Beck and Hall, 1999; Morales-Johansson et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Beck and Hall, 1999; Morales-Johansson et al., 2009).

claim: PP6 is proposed to dephosphorylate GCN2 when mTORC1 is inhibited in mammalian cells
source: PP6 is also proposed to dephosphorylate GCN2 when mTORC1 is inhibited in mammalian cells (Wengrod et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Wengrod et al., 2015).

claim: Active PP6 holoenzyme dephosphorylates phosphoSer145 in vitro
source: Active PP6 holoenzyme, but not the catalytically inactive mutant, dephosphorylated phosphoSer145, but not phosphoSer19 (Akt site) in vitro (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data (Figure 2d).

claim: PP6 does not dephosphorylate phosphoSer19 (Akt site) in vitro
source: Active PP6 holoenzyme, but not the catalytically inactive mutant, dephosphorylated phosphoSer145, but not phosphoSer19 (Akt site) in vitro (Figure 2d).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data showing no change in phospho-Ser19 (Figure 2d).

claim: Rapamycin treatment decreases phosphorylation of Ser145 and this is rescued by PPP6C knockdown
source: Importantly, rapamycin treatment of HEK293 cells decreased phosphorylation of Ser145 and this was rescued by PPP6C knockdown (Figure 2e,f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing maintained Ser145 phosphorylation with rapamycin in PPP6C knockdown cells (Figure 2e,f).

claim: Ser145 is phosphorylated by mTOR and dephosphorylated by PP6 in vivo
source: These data suggest that Ser145 is phosphorylated by mTOR and dephosphorylated by PP6 in vivo (Figure 2i).
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including in vitro assays and cellular experiments with rapamycin and PP6 knockdown.

claim: PP6 knockdown increases S6K phosphorylation
source: We also tested the effect of PP6 knock-down on known substrates of mTORC1 such as p-S6K, p-ULK1 and 4EBP1, and observed that while PP6 knockdown increases S6K phosphorylation, it does not affect ULK1 phosphorylation or 4EBP1 mobility shift (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased p-S6K upon PP6 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).

claim: PP6 knockdown does not affect ULK1 phosphorylation
source: We also tested the effect of PP6 knock-down on known substrates of mTORC1 such as p-S6K, p-ULK1 and 4EBP1, and observed that while PP6 knockdown increases S6K phosphorylation, it does not affect ULK1 phosphorylation or 4EBP1 mobility shift (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing no change in p-ULK1 upon PP6 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).

claim: PP6 knockdown does not affect 4EBP1 mobility shift
source: We also tested the effect of PP6 knock-down on known substrates of mTORC1 such as p-S6K, p-ULK1 and 4EBP1, and observed that while PP6 knockdown increases S6K phosphorylation, it does not affect ULK1 phosphorylation or 4EBP1 mobility shift (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing no change in 4EBP1 mobility upon PP6 knockdown (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).

claim: This is the first report of PP6-dependent changes in S6K phosphorylation
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of PP6-dependent changes in S6K phosphorylation.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Overexpression of untagged ZNRF2 significantly increased the activation of mTORC1 by amino acids
source: Furthermore, we investigated the role of ZNRF2 Ser145 phosphorylation on mTORC1 signaling and found that overexpression of untagged ZNRF2 significantly increased the activation of mTORC1 by amino acids
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing increased p-S6K upon ZNRF2 overexpression (Figure 2g).

claim: Overexpression of ZNRF2-Ser145Ala augmented the effect of ZNRF2 on mTORC1 activation
source: while overexpression of ZNRF2-Ser145Ala augmented this effect, suggesting that phosphorylation of Ser145 negatively regulates ZNRF2 function towards mTORC1 (Figure 2g,i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing greater p-S6K increase with Ser145Ala mutant (Figure 2g).

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser145 negatively regulates ZNRF2 function towards mTORC1
source: while overexpression of ZNRF2-Ser145Ala augmented this effect, suggesting that phosphorylation of Ser145 negatively regulates ZNRF2 function towards mTORC1 (Figure 2g,i and Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that preventing Ser145 phosphorylation enhances ZNRF2's positive effect on mTORC1.

claim: Augmented activation of mTORC1 by ZNRF2-Ser145Ala did not occur when the mutant also carried a Gly2Ala mutation
source: This augmented activation of mTORC1 did not occur when the overexpressed ZNRF2-Ser145Ala mutant also carried a Gly2Ala mutation, rendering ZNRF2 non-myristoylatable (Figure 2h).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing loss of enhanced mTORC1 activation with S145A/G2A double mutant (Figure 2h).

claim: Membranal localization of ZNRF2 is important for its effect on mTORC1 activation by amino acids
source: These findings suggest that both membranal localization of ZNRF2 and its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity are important for its effect on mTORC1 activation by amino acids.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the requirement of myristoylation (G2A mutation abolishes effect) for ZNRF2's function.

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligase activity of ZNRF2 is important for its effect on mTORC1 activation by amino acids
source: These findings suggest that both membranal localization of ZNRF2 and its E3 ubiquitin ligase activity are important for its effect on mTORC1 activation by amino acids.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing ligase-dead C199A mutation decreases ZNRF2's enhancement of mTORC1 activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).

claim: Activation of mTORC1 by amino acids was decreased in HeLa and HEK293 cells upon knockdown of ZNRF2
source: Activation of mTORC1 by amino acids was decreased in HeLa and HEK293 cells upon knockdown of ZNRF2, as detected by a decrease in phosphorylation of S6K and 4E-BP1 (Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing decreased p-S6K and 4E-BP1 phosphorylation in ZNRF2 knockdown cells (Figure 3a).

claim: mTOR-LAMP2 colocalization was reduced by 30% upon knockdown of ZNRF2
source: The mTOR-LAMP2 colocalization was reduced by 30% upon knockdown of ZNRF2 (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data (Figure 3b,c).

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown resulted in decreased cell proliferation in HeLa cells
source: Moreover, ZNRF2 knockdown resulted in decreased cell proliferation and cell size in HeLa cells (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell viability assay data (Figure 3d).

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown resulted in decreased cell size in HeLa cells
source: Moreover, ZNRF2 knockdown resulted in decreased cell proliferation and cell size in HeLa cells (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown had no negative effect on activation of the PI 3-kinase pathway in response to IGF1
source: In contrast, ZNRF2 knockdown had no negative effect on activation of the PI 3-kinase pathway in response to IGF1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing maintained or increased Akt phosphorylation in ZNRF2 knockdown cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown increases phosphorylation of Ser473 and Thr308 of Akt
source: In fact, we noticed an increase in the phosphorylation of Ser473 and Thr308 of Akt and a decrease in the phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, upon ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f).

claim: Lower mTORC1 signalling relieves negative feedback via IRS1 and Grb10
source: In fact, we noticed an increase in the phosphorylation of Ser473 and Thr308 of Akt and a decrease in the phosphorylation of 4E-BP1, upon ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1f), consistent with lower mTORC1 signalling relieving negative feedback via IRS1 and Grb10 (Harrington et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2011; Manning, 2004; Shah et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature describing mTORC1 negative feedback mechanisms (Harrington et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2011; Manning, 2004; Shah et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2011).

claim: V0A1/A2 components of the V-ATPase and p18 subunit of Ragulator were identified with high scores in ZNRF2-GFP immunoprecipitates
source: In particular, the V0A1/A2 components of the V-ATPase and p18 subunit of Ragulator were identified with high scores.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1).

claim: V0D1, V1A, V0C and V1E subunits of V-ATPase were identified with relatively lower scores in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates
source: Other V-ATPase subunits, namely V0D1, V1A, V0C and V1E; and the Mp1 and p14 subunits of Ragulator were also identified with relatively lower scores (Figure 4a and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1).

claim: Mp1 and p14 subunits of Ragulator were identified with relatively lower scores in ZNRF2 immunoprecipitates
source: Other V-ATPase subunits, namely V0D1, V1A, V0C and V1E; and the Mp1 and p14 subunits of Ragulator were also identified with relatively lower scores (Figure 4a and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data (Figure 4a, Supplementary file 1).

claim: V0A2 and p18 co-purified with C-terminally tagged ZNRF2-GFP but not N-terminally tagged GFP-ZNRF2
source: Similar to mTOR, V0A2 and p18 co-purified with C-terminally tagged ZNRF2-GFP, but not N-terminally tagged GFP-ZNRF2 (Figure 4b)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4b).

claim: V0A2 and p18 do not co-purify with the Gly2Ala myristoylation-defective mutant of ZNRF2
source: nor with the Gly2Ala myristoylation-defective mutant of ZNRF2 (Figure 4c), indicating that myristoylation of ZNRF2 and/or its localization to membranes is required for its binding to V-ATPase and p18.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4c).

claim: Myristoylation of ZNRF2 and/or its localization to membranes is required for its binding to V-ATPase and p18
source: nor with the Gly2Ala myristoylation-defective mutant of ZNRF2 (Figure 4c), indicating that myristoylation of ZNRF2 and/or its localization to membranes is required for its binding to V-ATPase and p18.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of binding with myristoylation-defective mutant.

claim: Ligase-dead ZNRF2 (Cys199Ala) displayed decreased binding to V0A2 and p18
source: The ligase-dead ZNRF2 (Cys199Ala) also displayed decreased binding to V0A2 and p18 (Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data (Figure 4b).

claim: V0A2 and p18 bind to ZNRF2 mainly through the N-terminal region of ZNRF2 (residues 1–156)
source: Similar to mTOR, V0A2 and p18 also bind to ZNRF2 mainly through the N-terminal region of ZNRF2 (residues 1–156), although residual binding was also observed with the RING domain N-terminally fused to the N-myristoylation motif (Figure 4e).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data with ZNRF2 fragments (Figure 4e).

claim: The binding of ZNRF2 to V-ATPase is specific and occurs at the membranes
source: These experiments indicate that the binding of ZNRF2 to V-ATPase is specific and occurs at the membranes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experiments showing myristoylation-dependent binding and domain mapping.

claim: Binding of ZNRF2 to V0A2 was enhanced when cells were treated with bafilomycin A
source: The binding of ZNRF2 to V0A2 was enhanced when cells were treated with bafilomycin A (Baf.) or concanamycin A (Con A), specific V-ATPase inhibitors (Figure 4c and 4d, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing increased V0A2 binding with bafilomycin treatment (Figure 4c).

claim: Binding of ZNRF2 to V0A2 was enhanced when cells were treated with concanamycin A
source: The binding of ZNRF2 to V0A2 was enhanced when cells were treated with bafilomycin A (Baf.) or concanamycin A (Con A), specific V-ATPase inhibitors (Figure 4c and 4d, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing increased V0A2 binding with concanamycin treatment (Figure 4d).

claim: The interactions of ZNRF2 with V-ATPase and Ragulator were not markedly regulated by amino acids
source: However, the interactions of ZNRF2 with V-ATPase and Ragulator were not markedly regulated by amino acids (Figure 4c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing similar binding with or without amino acids (Figure 4c).

claim: Knockdown of p18 did not affect interaction of ZNRF2-GFP with V0A2
source: Knockdown of p18 did not affect interaction of ZNRF2-GFP with V0A2, whereas knockdown of V0A2 decreased the levels of p18 in ZNRF2-GFP immunoprecipitates (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in p18 knockdown cells (Figure 4f).

claim: Knockdown of V0A2 decreased the levels of p18 in ZNRF2-GFP immunoprecipitates
source: Knockdown of p18 did not affect interaction of ZNRF2-GFP with V0A2, whereas knockdown of V0A2 decreased the levels of p18 in ZNRF2-GFP immunoprecipitates (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data in V0A2 knockdown cells (Figure 4f).

claim: Binding of ZNRF2 to V-ATPase is likely to be direct and not mediated by p18
source: Thus, binding of ZNRF2 to V-ATPase is likely to be direct and not mediated by p18.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that p18 knockdown does not affect ZNRF2-V0A2 interaction.

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown did not alter the elution profiles of the V0 and V1 subunits of V-ATPase
source: ZNRF2 knockdown did not alter the elution profiles of the V0 and V1 subunits of V-ATPase, as assessed by size-exclusion chromatography, suggesting that ZNRF2 does not affect the association between V0 and V1 compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).

claim: ZNRF2 does not affect the association between V0 and V1 compartments
source: ZNRF2 knockdown did not alter the elution profiles of the V0 and V1 subunits of V-ATPase, as assessed by size-exclusion chromatography, suggesting that ZNRF2 does not affect the association between V0 and V1 compartments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is inferred from unchanged elution profiles of V-ATPase subunits upon ZNRF2 knockdown.

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown caused no significant changes in the elution profiles of Ragulator subunit p18, mTOR, raptor or rictor
source: Likewise, ZNRF2 knockdown caused no significant changes in the elution profiles of Ragulator subunit p18, mTOR, raptor or rictor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: The claim is supported by size-exclusion chromatography data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown did not alter the protein levels of V-ATPase or Ragulator
source: ZNRF2 knockdown did not alter the protein levels of V-ATPase or Ragulator (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).

claim: Lack of ZNRF2 does not compromise the abundance or formation of V-ATPase and mTORC1 complexes
source: These experiments suggest that lack of ZNRF2 does not compromise the abundance or formation of V-ATPase and mTORC1 complexes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from size-exclusion chromatography and protein level data showing no changes in complex formation or abundance.

claim: De novo synthesis of V-ATPase and its trafficking from ER to lysosomes is required for recovery from ConA treatment
source: ConA binds tightly to V-ATPase and it has been proposed that de novo synthesis of the pump (and therefore its trafficking from ER to lysosomes) is required for the recovery from the ConA treatment (Hanada et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hanada et al., 1990).

claim: Recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown
source: We found that the recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA or BFA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 5a,b, respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced p-S6K recovery in ZNRF2 knockdown cells after ConA washout (Figure 5a).

claim: Recovery of mTORC1 activity after BFA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown
source: We found that the recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA or BFA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 5a,b, respectively)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing reduced p-S6K recovery in ZNRF2 knockdown cells after BFA washout (Figure 5b).

claim: Recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA chase was enhanced by ZNRF2-Ser145Ala overexpression
source: We found that the recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA or BFA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 5a,b, respectively), and enhanced by ZNRF2-Ser145Ala overexpression (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing enhanced p-S6K recovery with Ser145Ala overexpression after ConA washout (Figure 5c).

claim: Recovery of mTORC1 activity after BFA chase was enhanced by ZNRF2-Ser145Ala overexpression
source: We found that the recovery of mTORC1 activity after ConA or BFA chase was markedly attenuated by ZNRF2 knockdown (Figure 5a,b, respectively), and enhanced by ZNRF2-Ser145Ala overexpression (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing enhanced p-S6K recovery with Ser145Ala overexpression after BFA washout (Figure 5d).

claim: Knockdown of ZNRF2 resulted in decreased association of V-ATPase with lysosomes
source: Consistent with the ConA and BFA chase experiments, the knockdown of ZNRF2 resulted in decreased association of V-ATPase with lysosomes (the LAMP2 containing compartment) when V0A2 was immunopurified in the presence of a cross-linking agent (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation data showing reduced LAMP2 co-purification with V0A2 in ZNRF2 knockdown cells (Figure 5e).

claim: In cells depleted of ZNRF2, lysosomal pH increased from 4.3 to 5.5 in cells grown under standard conditions
source: In cells depleted of ZNRF2, we observed a marked increase in the lysosomal pH from 4.3 up to 5.5 in cells grown under standard conditions, and from 4.7 to 6 in amino acid-starved cells (Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurement data using Dextran-Oregon Green (Figure 5f).

claim: In cells depleted of ZNRF2, lysosomal pH increased from 4.7 to 6 in amino acid-starved cells
source: In cells depleted of ZNRF2, we observed a marked increase in the lysosomal pH from 4.3 up to 5.5 in cells grown under standard conditions, and from 4.7 to 6 in amino acid-starved cells (Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b)
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurement data (Figure 5f).

claim: ZNRF2 is crucial for the V-ATPase function
source: In cells depleted of ZNRF2, we observed a marked increase in the lysosomal pH from 4.3 up to 5.5 in cells grown under standard conditions, and from 4.7 to 6 in amino acid-starved cells (Figure 5f and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), indicating that ZNRF2 is crucial for the V-ATPase function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that ZNRF2 knockdown increases lysosomal pH, indicating impaired V-ATPase function.

claim: Overexpression of constitutively-active RagBGTP-RagCGDP complex renders mTORC1 insensitive to amino acid deprivation
source: To test whether ZNRF2 acts upstream of Rag-GTPases, we used a constitutively-active RagBGTP-RagCGDP complex (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008) that renders mTORC1 insensitive to amino acid deprivation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2008; Sancak et al., 2008) and Western blot data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).

claim: Overexpression of constitutively-active Rag mutants rescued the decrease in mTORC1 activity caused by ZNRF2 knockdown
source: Overexpression of these Rag mutants rescued the decrease in mTORC1 activity caused by ZNRF2 knockdown, suggesting that ZNRF2 acts upstream of the Rag GTPases.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data showing restored p-S6K in ZNRF2 knockdown cells expressing active Rag mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).

claim: ZNRF2 acts upstream of the Rag GTPases
source: Overexpression of these Rag mutants rescued the decrease in mTORC1 activity caused by ZNRF2 knockdown, suggesting that ZNRF2 acts upstream of the Rag GTPases.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the rescue experiment with constitutively active Rag mutants.

claim: ZNRF2 contributes to mTORC1 activation by amino acids upstream of V-ATPase and Rag GTPases, via regulating V-ATPase localization and function
source: These experiments reinforce a model in which ZNRF2 contributes to mTORC1 activation by amino acids upstream of V-ATPase and Rag GTPases, via regulating V-ATPase localization and function (Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including V-ATPase trafficking, pH measurements, and Rag rescue experiments.

claim: ZNRF2 is a new binding partner of mTOR
source: In this study, we identified a new binding partner of mTOR, ZNRF2, which acts as a positive effector functioning upstream of V-ATPase to mediate amino acid-activation of mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry and immunoprecipitation data showing ZNRF2-mTOR interaction.

claim: ZNRF2 acts as a positive effector functioning upstream of V-ATPase to mediate amino acid-activation of mTORC1
source: In this study, we identified a new binding partner of mTOR, ZNRF2, which acts as a positive effector functioning upstream of V-ATPase to mediate amino acid-activation of mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing ZNRF2's effects on V-ATPase function and mTORC1 activation.

claim: ZNRF2 is a new substrate of mTORC1 and PP6 that promotes negative feedback regulation of mTORC1
source: Furthermore, we show that ZNRF2 is also a new substrate of mTORC1 and PP6 that promotes negative feedback regulation of mTORC1 (Figure 2i and Figure 5g).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinase and phosphatase assays, and functional data showing Ser145 phosphorylation negatively regulates ZNRF2 function.

claim: ZNRF2 is conserved among eukaryotes
source: Similar to mTOR, ZNRF2 is conserved among eukaryotes (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Putative ZNRF2 orthologues in S. cerevisiae (Pib1p), D. melanogaster, C. elegans and vertebrates share most similarity in their UBZ and RING E3 ligase domains
source: Putative ZNRF2 orthologues in S. cerevisiae (Pib1p), D. melanogaster, C. elegans and vertebrates share most similarity in their UBZ and RING E3 ligase domains.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).

claim: D. melanogaster and C. elegans orthologues of ZNRF2 have a conserved N-myristoylation signal
source: The D. melanogaster and C. elegans orthologues of ZNRF2 also have a conserved N-myristoylation signal, which is critical for membranal localization of ZNRF2.
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).

claim: The S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for ZNRF2 orthologue Pib1p has abnormal vacuolar morphology
source: Notably, the S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for ZNRF2 orthologue Pib1p has abnormal vacuolar morphology, increased replicative lifespan and decreased growth in minimal medium, indicative of roles analogous to the V-ATPase- and mTOR-related functions of ZNRF2 that we describe in this study (http://www.yeastgenome.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by information from the Saccharomyces Genome Database (http://www.yeastgenome.org).

claim: The S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for Pib1p has increased replicative lifespan
source: Notably, the S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for ZNRF2 orthologue Pib1p has abnormal vacuolar morphology, increased replicative lifespan and decreased growth in minimal medium, indicative of roles analogous to the V-ATPase- and mTOR-related functions of ZNRF2 that we describe in this study (http://www.yeastgenome.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by information from the Saccharomyces Genome Database.

claim: The S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for Pib1p has decreased growth in minimal medium
source: Notably, the S288C strain of S. cerevisiae that carries a null allele for ZNRF2 orthologue Pib1p has abnormal vacuolar morphology, increased replicative lifespan and decreased growth in minimal medium, indicative of roles analogous to the V-ATPase- and mTOR-related functions of ZNRF2 that we describe in this study (http://www.yeastgenome.org).
evidence: The claim is supported by information from the Saccharomyces Genome Database.

claim: ZNRF2 is targeted via N-myristoylation to Golgi and other intracellular membranes where it interacts with the V-ATPase
source: Our data suggest that ZNRF2 is targeted via N-myristoylation to Golgi and other intracellular membranes where it interacts with the V-ATPase.
evidence: The claim is supported by imaging data showing Golgi localization and immunoprecipitation data showing V-ATPase interaction.

claim: ZNRF2 promotes the trafficking of newly-synthesized V-ATPase to the lysosomes
source: However, several observations indicate that ZNRF2 promotes the trafficking of newly-synthesized V-ATPase to the lysosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from ConA/BFA chase experiments and decreased V-ATPase-lysosome association upon ZNRF2 knockdown.

claim: ZNRF2 is a key regulator of V-ATPase trafficking
source: These data suggest that ZNRF2 is a key regulator of V-ATPase trafficking, impacting on its key function of maintaining vesicle pH.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including trafficking assays and pH measurements.

claim: Lysosomes are acidic (pH ~4.5) intracellular organelles
source: Lysosomes are acidic (pH ~4.5) intracellular organelles and their primary function is degradation of extracellular and intracellular material (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).

claim: The primary function of lysosomes is degradation of extracellular and intracellular material
source: Lysosomes are acidic (pH ~4.5) intracellular organelles and their primary function is degradation of extracellular and intracellular material (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Settembre et al., 2013).

claim: ZNRF2 depletion decreased mTORC1 signalling, consistent with requirement of functional lysosomes to sustain mTORC1 activation
source: Concomitantly with increased lysosomal pH, ZNRF2 depletion decreased mTORC1 signalling, consistent with requirement of functional lysosomes to sustain mTORC1 activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between increased lysosomal pH and decreased mTORC1 activity upon ZNRF2 knockdown.

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown affects the lysosomal recruitment of mTORC1
source: We also demonstrate that ZNRF2 knockdown affects the lysosomal recruitment of mTORC1, which is mediated by the Rag GTPases, the Ragulator complex and the V-ATPase.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing decreased mTOR-LAMP2 colocalization (Figure 3b,c).

claim: Zoncu et al. (2011) proposed an inside-out mechanism for sensing amino acids that requires the V-ATPase
source: Zoncu et al. (2011) proposed an inside-out mechanism for sensing amino acids that requires the V-ATPase, which in turns interacts with the Ragulator complex.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Zoncu et al., 2011).

claim: Attenuation of mTORC1 recruitment to the lysosomal membranes upon ZNRF2 knockdown is due to impaired function of V-ATPase and subsequent effects on the Ragulator and Rag GTPases
source: We therefore hypothesize that attenuation of mTORC1 recruitment to the lysosomal membranes upon ZNRF2 knockdown is due to impaired function of V-ATPase and subsequent effects on the Ragulator and Rag GTPases.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis inferred from multiple observations about ZNRF2's effects on V-ATPase and mTORC1.

claim: ZNRF2 is a positive regulator of mTORC1
source: As well as being a positive regulator of mTORC1, ZNRF2 is also a new target of negative regulation by mTORC1, indicative of a self-regulating feedback mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing ZNRF2 knockdown decreases mTORC1 activity and overexpression increases it.

claim: ZNRF2 is a target of negative regulation by mTORC1
source: As well as being a positive regulator of mTORC1, ZNRF2 is also a new target of negative regulation by mTORC1, indicative of a self-regulating feedback mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing mTORC1 phosphorylates ZNRF2 on Ser145, promoting its cytosolic translocation and reducing its positive effect on mTORC1.

claim: ZNRF2 was identified in an unbiased quantitative phosphoproteomics screen aiming to find mTOR substrates
source: Our findings are consistent with ZNRF2 having been identified in an unbiased quantitative phosphoproteomics screen aiming to find mTOR substrates (Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to published literature (Yu et al., 2011).

claim: mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of ZNRF2 on Ser145 enhances the release of ZNRF2 from intracellular membranes into the cytosol
source: Together with previous work (Hoxhaj et al., 2012), this study suggests that mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of ZNRF2 on Ser145 enhances the release of ZNRF2 from intracellular membranes into the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from this study and previous work (Hoxhaj et al., 2012) showing Ser145 phosphorylation correlates with cytosolic localization.

claim: The release of ZNRF2 from membranes limits the activation of mTORC1 in response to amino acids and growth factors
source: We therefore propose the existence of an auto-inhibitory feedback loop in which the release of ZNRF2 from membranes limits the activation of mTORC1 in response to amino acids and growth factors, perhaps preventing unrestrained cell growth.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on the observation that Ser145 phosphorylation promotes cytosolic translocation and negatively regulates ZNRF2 function.

claim: This finely balanced dynamic regulation of ZNRF2 is reminiscent of the negative feedbacks by mTORC1 via S6K on IRS1
source: This finely balanced dynamic regulation of ZNRF2 is reminiscent of the negative feedbacks by mTORC1 via S6K on IRS1 (Harrington et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2004) and Grb10 (Hsu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim draws an analogy to known mTORC1 feedback mechanisms supported by citations (Harrington et al., 2004; Shah et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2011).

claim: mTORC1 mediates release of ZNRF2 from membranes into the cytosol, resulting in decreased mTORC1 activity through lysosome basification via the V-ATPase pathway
source: In our model, mTORC1 mediate release of ZNRF2 from membranes into the cytosol, resulting in decreased mTORC1 activity through lysosome basification via the V-ATPase pathway.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model integrating multiple observations about ZNRF2 phosphorylation, localization, and effects on V-ATPase and mTORC1.

claim: Hampering activation of mTORC1 by amino acids during strong activation by growth factors/insulin may ensure that hyperactivation of mTORC1 does not occur
source: Hampering activation of mTORC1 by amino acids, during strong activation of the pathway by growth factors/insulin, may ensure that hyperactivation of mTORC1 does not occur.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation of the negative feedback mechanism.

claim: ZNRF2 knockdown results in decreased mTORC1 signalling in cells lacking TSC2 that have constitutively active mTORC1
source: Consistent with this proposal, ZNRF2 knockdown results in decreased mTORC1 signalling in cells lacking TSC2, that have constitutively active mTORC1 (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is stated but data are not shown in the manuscript.

claim: ZNRF2 adjusts the homeostatic set point for mTORC1
source: In other words, ZNRF2 adjusts the homeostatic set point for mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is an interpretive statement about ZNRF2's overall role in mTORC1 regulation.

claim: PP6 is a positive regulator of ZNRF2 by promoting its rebinding to membranes
source: We also show that the mTORC1-phosphorylated Ser145 on ZNRF2 is dephosphorylated by PP6, making PP6 a positive regulator of ZNRF2 by promoting its rebinding to membranes where it can regulate the V-ATPase and mTORC1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from PP6's dephosphorylation of Ser145 and the observation that Ser145 phosphorylation promotes cytosolic translocation.

claim: The relative activity of PP6 versus mTORC1 will set the level of membrane bound ZNRF2, mTORC1 activity and cell growth
source: PhosphoSer145 of ZNRF2 should provide a useful reporter for studying how PP6 is regulated, which is critical because the relative activity of PP6 versus mTORC1 will set the level of membrane bound ZNRF2, mTORC1 activity and cell growth.
evidence: The claim is a speculative statement about the regulatory balance between PP6 and mTORC1.

claim: ZNRF2 is a positive regulator of nutrient-mediated mTORC1 signalling
source: In summary, this study introduces ZNRF2 as a positive regulator of mTORC1 activation by amino acids, which functions upstream of the V-ATPase and of Rag-GTPases.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experiments showing ZNRF2's positive effects on amino acid-stimulated mTORC1 activation.

claim: ZNRF2 functions upstream of the V-ATPase and of Rag-GTPases
source: In summary, this study introduces ZNRF2 as a positive regulator of mTORC1 activation by amino acids, which functions upstream of the V-ATPase and of Rag-GTPases.
evidence: The claim is supported by V-ATPase trafficking data and Rag rescue experiments.

claim: ZNRF2 is a negative feedback target of mTORC1 signalling
source: ZNRF2 is also identified as a negative feedback target of mTORC1 signalling.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing mTORC1 phosphorylates ZNRF2 on Ser145, promoting its inactivation.
